scientific_teacher_note: Ideal open-tank Torricelli efflux v=√(98)=9.90 m/s at head 5m with g=9.8. Surface speed, extra applied pressure and losses are neglected.
Ideal efflux v=√(24.5)=4.95 m/s for 1.25m head; this assumes identical atmospheric pressures at the tank surface and outlet.

The calculation h=v²/(2g)=10m is correct as equivalent velocity head or driving elevation head for ideal Torricelli efflux. But calling it 'pressure head' without identifying the pressure datum can confuse pressure head P/(rho g) with the velocity head. Teacher should clarify terminology before formal exam certification.
v=√39.2=6.26 m/s under ideal open-tank/free-jet assumptions; not a universal measured real-orifice speed with viscous losses.

v2=3.0 m/s follows directly from steady incompressible Q=A v, not a Bernoulli pressure relation. Source author assigns B40 Application, but this item independently tests summative continuity SLO B36; B44 device context alone is insufficient for automatic certification.

v2=6.0 m/s from the area ratio 8/2 and inlet speed 1.5m/s; the squared-cm area ratio cancels. This is a single continuity calculation B36 candidate even though the device is called a Venturi meter; the original B40 tag is not item certified.
P1−P2=500(36−4)=16000 Pa. Original B has the proper sign; the result requires lossless same-height Bernoulli along a common streamline.
Ideal same-height Bernoulli yields P1−P2=400(25−4)=8400 Pa, original D; no pump-head or appreciable viscous dissipation.
v2=√13≈3.61 m/s, original B. Positive P1−P2 means higher speed at the downstream Venturi throat under the ideal horizontal model.

Two same-fluid, static piezometer columns with equal datum have a 2.5m difference giving ΔP=24500 Pa. This directly tests hydrostatic pressure head measurement, not on its own using the Bernoulli pressure-speed-height equation for two flowing sections; B40 or B44 item scope must be assessed individually.
NBF printed p104 Eq6.29 matches v1=√[11.76/(4−1)]=√3.92≈1.98 m/s with r=A1/A2=2. Same-density piezometer liquid, horizontal lossless Venturi and steady discharge are assumed.
Printed Venturi relation gives v1=√[15.68/(9−1)]=√1.96=1.40m/s. The measurement-head and area ratio refer to equal-elevation steady ideal flow.

Q=(5.0×10^-4 m²)(4.0m/s)=2.0×10^-3 m³/s. Area unit conversion is essential; this is a one-section volumetric flow / continuity prerequisite, not independently an application of Bernoulli pressure to water flow as B40 demands.
P1−P2=500(25−9)=8000 Pa=8.0 kPa. Original B follows ideal horizontal along-streamline Bernoulli and a positive pressure drop for acceleration.
Printed original NBF Example6.4 p105 confirms v1=4m/s, v2=3m/s, initial 47.1kPa and second point 3m lower; ideal P2=47.1+3.5+29.4=80.0kPa. Original source B exactly matches printed result.

ρgΔh=(1000)(9.8)(3)=29400Pa=29.4kPa, source D. Calculating only the gravitational-energy density term is useful supporting practice, but is not itself full B40 Application of horizontal/vertical Bernoulli across two flow points.

Original printed NBF Assignment6.4 p106 truly gives 450m/s above and 410m/s below with air density 1.29kg/m³; the specified simplified Bernoulli calculation gives ΔP=22188Pa, source C. Both speeds exceed typical near-room-temperature air sound speed (~340m/s): actual flows are compressible and may involve shock waves, so incompressible wing-velocity pressure inference cannot represent a realistic aerodynamic prediction. Retain clearly as textbook idealization, not a measured real lift estimate.

Printed original Assignment6.4 states 15m ×3m, with source ideal ΔP=22188Pa; F=22188×45=998460N exactly, original B. The simple uniform ΔP across projected area neglects actual distribution; moreover upstream 450/410m/s speeds are supersonic for usual air conditions, invalidating incompressible Bernoulli realism. Keep the textbook arithmetic but require conceptual caveat for exam suitability.

F≈1500Pa×20m²=30000N is valid as an approximation when 1500Pa is the representative pressure difference over the 20m² effective surface. Real lift requires spatial pressure integration and may include shear.

The arithmetic ΔP=0.6(900−400)=300Pa is correct in the simplified textbook wing model at the supplied 30/20m/s speeds (source A), but comparing local velocities above and below different streamlines only fixes pressure difference when a common upstream total head/Bernoulli constant and appropriate elevations, losses and flow fields are assumed. Do not infer pressure difference from speeds alone universally.
